publications.title: Identifiable Regime Detection in Pension-Fund Networks via Sticky Hidden Markov Models
publications.authors: Megang Nkamga Junile Staures;Kabašinskas, Audrius
publications.summary: We document a network-level vulnerability in pension-fund systems: lifecycle allocation regulation, designed to protect individual participants, compresses cross-fund return dynamics to the point where provider choice offers little diversification. Using daily net asset value data from second-pillar pension funds in Lithuania over 2019–2025, we found that a single common factor explains more than 72% of total return variance even in the calmest observed periods. We develop an unsupervised regime-detection framework that combines a PCA-based absorption ratio, DTW-based hierarchical clustering, and a Gaussian hidden Markov model with a data-driven crisis threshold. The HMM specification is supported by a dual empirical calibration of the stickiness prior, and its emission estimates agree closely with a fully Bayesian sticky-HMM specification. The framework identifies three latent regimes in which elevated systemic co-movement is the structural norm rather than an exceptional state and shows that funds separate first by lifecycle segment (conservative versus growth cohorts) and only secondarily by provider, with no single label axis reproducing the structure on its own. The absorption ratio has no significant relationship with global equity benchmarks in either calm or high-concentration regimes, indicating that the detected regimes are not explained by the external benchmarks considered, including global equity indices and a euro-area rate/bond proxy. Cluster-level mean-absolute-active return amplification of 1.06× to 1.33× during high-concentration episodes confirms that even conservative funds serving retirement-age participants are not insulated.

publications.title: A Multimodal Vision-Language Framework for Financial Anomaly Detection
publications.authors: Jheng, Siang-Li;Pele, Daniel Traian;Tak, Rahul;Gaman, Ștefan
publications.subjects: Anomaly Detection;Large Language Models;Multimodal AI;Market Regime Classification;Time-Series Analysis
publications.summary: Financial markets are complex systems where state estimation typically relies on either quantitative time-series models or subjective technical analysis. A gap remains in bridging scalable quantitative methods with the pattern-recognition intuition of human experts. In this work, we introduce a multimodal vision-language framework for financial anomaly detection that explores reframing market regime classification as a visual recognition task using advanced multimodal AI. We propose a methodology to project high-dimensional market indicators onto a standardized, multi-panel image format. We leverage the zero-shot capability of state-of-the-art Vision Language Models (VLMs), specifically GPT-4.1. We employ a rolling quantile-based approach for programmatic data labelling to reduce subjectivity. Furthermore, to address the need for transparency, our framework extracts structured natural language rationales directly from the model, offering interpretable insights alongside classifications. Our results, validated through out-of-sample testing on the S&P500, suggest that this multimodal prompting approach achieves promising fidelity in detecting systemic anomalies, indicating its potential as a reliable and interpretable framework for financial AI.

publications.title: Can Foundation Models Manage Risk? Zero-Shot VaR and ES Forecasting with Conformal Calibration in CEE Markets
publications.authors: Jheng, Siang-Li;Tak, Rahul;Găman, Ștefan;Mazurencu-Marinescu-Pele, Miruna;Pele, Daniel Traian
publications.subjects: Value-at-Risk;Expected Shortfall;foundation models;time series forecasting;emerging markets;Central and Eastern Europe;backtesting;conformal prediction
publications.summary: Through this study, we assess the performance of three different time series foundation models (TSFMs) in producing regulatory-grade Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES) forecasts under a zero-shot setting. The daily returns cover five Central and Eastern European (CEE) markets, whose data are under-represented in standard time-series pre-training corpora. Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, and Moirai 2.0 compete against the well-known benchmarks GJR-GARCH, Historical Simulation, and conformal prediction wrappers for ARIMA and LSTM. We validate the forecasts using Kupiec, Christoffersen, and Acerbi-Szekely tests, along with the Basel traffic light system. All three raw TSFMs achieve competitive Green zone rates in zero-shot mode, with Chronos-2 attaining 90%, matching GJR-GARCH. Applying a rolling conformal calibration wrapper to the TSFMs brings significant improvements, outperforming the traditional models. Therefore, in the context of regulatory risk management, the results suggest that conformal calibration is a critical component for deploying foundation models.

publications.title: Cryptocurrencies in a Changing Financial Landscape: A Systematic Review
publications.authors: Jheng, Siang-Li;Conda, Alexandra;Pele, Daniel Traian;Härdle, Wolfgang Karl
publications.subjects: Cryptocurrencies;Asset Allocation;Speculative Bubbles;Valuation Models;Index Construction;Digital Finance;Systematic Review
publications.summary: 2024 marks a significant milestone in integrating digital finance into the global financial landscape. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s approval of Bitcoin and Ethereum ETFs signaled wider mainstream adoption. Shortly thereafter, Donald Trump’s return to the presidency drove Bitcoin prices beyond $100,000. In light of these developments, we observe the rapid changes in cryptocurrency market prices, trends, and regulatory policies, which drive us to conduct a comprehensive review of cryptocurrencies asset’s literature and examine its robustness. Our study covers several themes: how cryptocurrencies fit into broader asset allocation strategies, techniques to create crypto-based indexes, current debates over speculative bubbles, and the evolution of valuation models to highlight the dual aspects of market opportunities and risks. Throughout our review, we compare previous studies with the latest data, seeking to determine which arguments continue to hold up and which require adjustment. Although digital assets have experienced multiple crashes, they often rebound more strongly than expected, making them a topic of intense debate among academics, regulators, and investors. We aim to assemble an organized summary of research findings, providing a comprehensive framework that unites historical evolution with recent shifts and future perspectives.

publications.title: BitMood: AI analysis of Bitcoin trends via Facebook emotions
publications.authors: Conda, Alexandra Ioana;Găman, Ștefan;Bâg, Raul Cristian;Mazurencu-Marinescu-Pele, Miruna;Pele, Daniel Traian;Härdle, Karl Wolfgang
publications.summary: This study investigates the relationship between Facebook sentiment and Bitcoin market dynamics using AI-based emotion detection. We analyze 120,000 Facebook posts collected via CrowdTangle alongside Bitcoin financial data from the Blockchain Research Center, covering 2015–2023. Employing FinBERT for sentiment classification, we develop novel compound sentiment scores that integrate text-based sentiment with Facebook’s multi-reaction engagement system, then apply four analytical components: sentiment analysis, Dynamic Topic Modeling, sentiment-based trading strategies, and machine learning volume prediction. Results demonstrate that Facebook sentiment has substantial predictive power for Bitcoin trading volume. Sentiment-based trading strategies significantly outperform buy-and-hold, achieving superior cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. For volume prediction, Linear Regression and Bidirectional LSTM achieve comparable test performance, indicating that model complexity does not guarantee superior prediction. Topic modeling reveals that cryptocurrency investment and trading discussions dominate Bitcoin discourse on Facebook, with themes evolving over time in response to market conditions. This research contributes by being the first to apply post-level NLP sentiment analysis of Facebook data to cryptocurrency markets, extending beyond the Twitter and Reddit focus of prior research. The findings provide practical tools for traders and analysts navigating volatile digital asset markets while demonstrating that Facebook’s demographically diverse user base and rich reaction system offer unique advantages for sentiment quantification.

publications.title: Causal Analysis for Time Series Foundation Models
publications.authors: Jander, Mathis;van Heeswijk, Wouter;Mes, Martijn
publications.summary: Transitioning from bespoke time series models towards time series foundation models changes the relationship of model and application from one-to-one to one-to-many. This shift introduces concentration risk as many, potentially high-risk, forecasting applications are exposed to the same biases and failure modes of a single time series foundation model. At the same time, this centralization allows for economies of scale in model development and validation. In this study we investigate how biases and failure modes of time series foundation models can be identified before deployment. We propose a causal analysis framework to investigate the ability of a time series foundation model to preserve time series patterns. To achieve this, we intervene on parameterized synthetic time series generators and measure the corresponding change in model output under ceteris paribus conditions. We apply our causal analysis framework to Chronos-2 and TimesFM-2.5 and test them across six distinct time series patterns. We find safe configurations for trend and harmonic oscillation patterns. The results also indicate a bias in both models towards overestimating persistence, sudden failures for both models against the regime switch pattern and failure for TimesFM-2.5 against the energy-release pattern. Our review of the original works for both models indicates that the findings might be explained by the data used for pretraining. We conclude our study with suggestions for further model development, recommendations for application-specific model selection, and a discussion of limitations and further research directions.

publications.title: Reinforcement Learning in Finance: A Systematic Literature Review of Research Frontiers and Methodological Trends
publications.authors: Jander, Mathis;van Heeswijk, Wouter;Mes, Martijn
publications.summary: This systematic literature review investigates current research frontiers in applying reinforcement learning (RL) to finance and catalogs methodological trends in the field. Using a structured Scopus search and a two-stage screening protocol, we identify 543 records and retain 163 studies (160 empirical, 3 reviews). Our analysis offers four contributions. First, we characterize the state of practice in terms of algorithmic focus, application domains, evaluation protocols, and deployment maturity. Second, we characterize prevalent methodological trends, observing variations in dataset diversity, evaluation depth, and metric consistency, while noting opportunities for enhanced reproducibility. Third, based on the evolution of the literature, we propose a task-based taxonomy that organizes the literature of RL applications in finance. Fourth, based on the findings, we suggest a framework for future research, emphasizing the potential benefits of standardized reporting protocols, data transparency, and high-fidelity environment modeling. We conclude that while RL in finance is experiencing rapid empirical growth, it currently exhibits a high degree of methodological fragmentation. Based on our findings, a transition toward integrated reporting standards and reproducible frameworks might be essential for the fields long-term maturity and its integration with financial economics.

publications.title: A Survey on Current Practices for Time Series Foundation Model Evaluation
publications.authors: Dilling, Ties;Jander, Mathis;Machado, Marcos Roberto;Ahmed, Faizan
publications.summary: Time series forecasting is present across several domains, such as finance, healthcare, energy, and operations, and foundation models promise to replace the traditional one-model-per-series workflow with a single zero-shot pretrained forecaster applied to these domains. Whether they deliver, and where they stop working, remains unknown. Following a survey (conducted on 1 June 2026 from Scopus) reported in line with the PRISMA guidelines, this study surveys 45 articles across five survey questions, covering what time series foundation models are and how they are designed and trained, how well they perform, what is known about their theoretical learnability limits, what phase diagrams and scaling laws reveal about them, and how controlled synthetic temporal environments are constructed and used to evaluate these models. A taxonomy of how models are built and how they are evaluated shows that the literature concentrates on building and benchmarking time series foundation models. Causal analysis of time series foundation models' abilities and limitations remains underexplored. We conclude that there is significant opportunity for future research in broadening the evaluation methods applied to time series foundation models.

publications.title: Racing the News: Nanosecond Market Efficiency at Eurex and CME
publications.authors: TAK, RAHUL;Schlamp, Stefan;Osterrieder, Joerg;Pele, Daniel Traian
publications.summary: We propose a Hybrid Piecewise Intensity model linking point-process econometrics to the physical architecture of electronic exchanges, decomposing trade arrivals in the 100 ms around macroeconomic announcements into four latency-aligned phases. Calibrated on nanosecond Eurex and CME data (2019--2025), modal Phase~1 peaks occur at 1.16 μs (Eurex) and 6.64 μs (CME), tracking each venue's network transmission floor. Comparing private embargo-based (PMI) and government-led (NFP, FOMC) releases, we find reaction-speed differences consistent with protocol-induced latency advantages, though confounds remain. The CME concentrates profitability within 200 μs with deteriorating risk-adjusted returns thereafter; Eurex sustains stable Sharpe ratios across longer horizons.

publications.title: AI Listening to Central Banks: From Words to Markets and Macroeconomic Outcomes
publications.authors: Amza, Antoaneta;TAK, RAHUL;Caliman, Stefan-Daniel;Pele, Daniel Traian
publications.summary: Central banks play a crucial role in maintaining economic stability and ensuring the proper functioning of financial markets. Their communication can significantly influence the economy by shaping market participants' perceptions and expectations. While most existing research on this topic focuses on the Federal Reserve or the European Central Bank, this paper provides a novel perspective by applying large language models to analyze the minutes of monetary policy meetings from Central and Eastern European central banks and their impact on key macroeconomic and financial indicators. The results show that, even for these economies, the informational content embedded in official communication has explanatory power, offering valuable insights for a region that remains relatively underexplored in the literature. The impact is particularly evident on the interbank money market, while the responses of other market segments are mixed, reflecting the predominantly bank-based structure of these financial systems. Furthermore, the analysis conducted through a Bayesian structural vector autoregression model (BSVAR) highlights a close link between central bank communication and macroeconomic developments in the studied economies. In particular, communication appears to be interpreted in a dual manner, reflecting both expectations of future monetary policy actions and information about underlying economic conditions. By documenting the relevance of communication shocks in Central and Eastern Europe, this paper extends the literature on monetary policy transmission

publications.title: LLM-Driven Stock Prediction: Capturing Market Trends with LLaMA
publications.authors: TAK, RAHUL;Pele, Daniel Traian
publications.summary: Stock price forecasting remains a challenging task due to the dynamic nature of financial markets and the influence of external factors such as investor sentiment and macroeconomic events. Traditional time series statistical models often struggle to capture complex nonlinear dependencies and market signals embedded in unstructured data. With advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs), it is now possible to integrate textual information from financial news, social media, and earnings reports to enhance predictive accuracy. In this study, we leverage the LLaMA family of LLMs to improve stock price forecasting by combining historical price with news. We evaluate the performance of LLaMA 3.3 against LLaMA 3.1 and the benchmark ARIMA model to assess its effectiveness in capturing time series patterns and textual signals. Our results indicate that LLaMA 3.3 outperforms both LLaMA 3.1 and ARIMA, demonstrating its superior capability in modeling complex financial relationships. Additionally, our analysis confirms that market sentiment has an impact on stock returns, with sentiments influencing short-term price fluctuations. By incorporating news sentiment in LLMs prompt, we achieve improved forecasts compared to models without news. This highlights the importance of integrating both structured (numerical time series) and unstructured (news sentiment) data for enhanced financial modeling. Our findings suggest that LLM-driven forecasting methods hold substantial promise for traders, analysts, and financial institutions seeking more accurate market predictions. Future work will explore fine-tuning LLaMA models for domain-specific financial tasks and improving interpretability in decision making processes.

publications.title: Quantlet: the code snippet knowledge platform
publications.authors: Găman, Ștefan;Winkel, Julian;Zuo, Xiaorui;Härdle, Karl Wolfgang;Pele, Daniel Traian
publications.summary: Many researchers increasingly rely on code snippets, algorithms, and information they find online to address complex problems. While these resources can provide immediate solutions, they often come from unverified sources and lack the context necessary for correct application. This growing dependence on readily available, sometimes ill-advised, information can lead to significant missteps, including inefficient code, flawed methodologies, or incorrect conclusions. As a result, researchers may unwittingly propagate errors or overlook more robust, appropriate solutions that are crucial for scientific progress. This paper presents the integration of the Quantlet and Quantinar platforms, collectively referred to as the Q2 ecosystem, aimed at overcoming challenges faced by applied scientists and researchers due to the vast and fragmented array of data and code available online. The focus of this integration is to enhance accessibility and usability of academic resources by effectively linking research with pertinent code and datasets. The study introduces an adaptive clustering algorithm that organizes and dynamically groups academic content from Quantinar alongside code and computational results from Quantlet, thus linking academic theory and practice. With these technical advancements, the Q2 framework aspires to enhance transparency and reproducibility within the academic research landscape. Ultimately, it aims to provide a cohesive learning environment that meets the evolving needs of the academic community, empowering researchers in their pursuit of knowledge and facilitating deeper insights into complex data-driven methodologies.

publications.title: ESG-Aware Asset Selection and Portfolio Optimization: A Comparative Study of Multi-Criteria Decision-Making Methods
publications.authors: Găman, Ștefan;Tak, Rahul;Jheng, Siang-Li;Pele, Daniel Traian
publications.summary: Besides the main goal of investment, which is to obtain profit, investors are also paying more attention to the broader impact of their choices. This awareness is reflected in portfolio construction, where environmental, social, and governance (ESG) scores are included alongside financial considerations. In this study, we propose a two-stage portfolio construction framework that uses ESG factors while separating asset selection from portfolio optimization, thereby allowing the effects of sustainability factors to be examined at both levels. Using a universe of 418 U.S. equities with ESG scores and sector classifications, assets are screened and ranked using three multi-criteria decision-making methods (AHP, TOPSIS, and VIKOR), based on ESG score, expected return, and volatility, while also ensuring sector balance. In the second stage, the selected asset universes are optimized in a mean-variance framework, producing classical, green (high ESG), and brown (low ESG) efficient frontiers. The findings indicate that ESG constraints have only a limited effect on portfolio efficiency. Green portfolios show similar risk-adjusted performance to classical portfolios. The asset selection methods mainly influence the composition and risk of the portfolios. VIKOR-based portfolios are more stable, TOPSIS-based portfolios are more volatile, and AHP portfolios are between these two cases. Overall, the results suggest that portfolio outcomes depend on both the asset selection method and the way sustainability constraints are introduced during optimization.

publications.title: Do Investors Buy Innovation: Market Responses to Ethereum Development Milestones
publications.authors: Lin, Min-Bin;Găman, Ștefan;Wang, Ruting;Pele, Daniel Traian
publications.summary: This paper studies how governance-driven technological innovation affects price discovery and market stability. Using Ethereum protocol upgrades as a natural laboratory, we combine event study and synthetic control methods to identify two distinct channels through which innovation impacts markets: cumulative abnormal returns (CAR), capturing growth-enhancing effects on expected fundamentals, and realized volatility (RV), reflecting short-term fragility from uncertainty and learning. We document substantial heterogeneity across upgrade types. Well-anticipated upgrades—such as Berlin, Gray Glacier, and Shanghai-Capella—generate positive CAR without increasing RV, consistent with an “innovation-growth” pattern. Muir Glacier simultaneously raises CAR and reduces RV by resolving near-term uncertainty, while Altair increases RV without affecting CAR, illustrating “innovation-fragility” during the live implementation of untested mechanisms. We further show that major upgrades induce cross-market herding, suggesting that protocol-level shocks propagate across crypto assets. Our findings offer insights for investors, platform developers, and regulators concerned with the stability of decentralized financial markets and their growing links to traditional finance.

publications.title: Decarbonizing the S&P 500: Sectoral Trade-offs Under Tracking-Error Constraints
publications.authors: Di Francesco, Rebecca;Hadji Misheva, Branka;Gomez Teijeiro, Lucia;Kurpisz, Adam
publications.summary: Climate change is increasingly recognized as a systemic financial risk, leading institutional investors to pursue portfolio decarbonization as a means of hedging climate-related risk while remaining closely aligned with benchmark indices. While prior work examines the carbon-tracking-error trade-off at the aggregate portfolio level, less is known about how this trade-off varies across sectors. This paper proposes a sector-level post-optimization framework to assess the feasibility of decarbonization under benchmark trackingerror constraints. It evaluates sectoral readiness along four dimensions-Room for Maneuver, Flexibility, Sensitivity, and Robustness-aggregated into a Decarbonization Readiness Index (DRI). Empirically, we document substantial cross-sector heterogeneity in early decarbonization potential, the diversity of feasible portfolio reallocations, the stability of optimized allocations, and the out-of-sample reliability of outcomes. These findings indicate that decarbonization opportunities are structurally uneven across sectors and that climatehedging effectiveness varies accordingly, highlighting the importance of a sector-specific perspective for institutional investors.

working_papers.title: Polymarked: Imporving physical density estimation with prediction markets
working_papers.authors: David Siang-Li Jheng;Owen Chaffard;Andrei-Theodor Ginavar;Stefan Gaman;Rahul Tak
working_papers.summary:
Using data from Polymarket's prediction markets on BTC prices and maturity matched Deribit BTC options, we evaluate whether prediction markets contain information relevant to physical density estimation beyond that of historical returns and traditional options. 

First results compare Deribit derivatives with prediction markets observed through the derivatives lens (a market in Polymarket is a Digital call option). Evidence of volatility smiles at short time to maturity is highlighted in both markets, while polymarket's smile tends to be more symmetric (no smirk). This is further supported by calibration analysis showing prediction markets to be better calibrated ( beat both historical methods and Deribit on Brier/log score). Mincer-Zarnowitz regression does highligh longshot bias expected in betting situations.

working_papers.title: Hierarchical Morphology Search
working_papers.summary: We seek to extend the current framework for hierarchical/grouped time series forecasting and linear reconciliation. We highlight using the proof of the MinTrace optimal projection that aggregates serve as additional noisy observations of the bottom nodes' errors. Thus aggregate forecasts are only useful if their disagreement with bottom forecasts are informative of bottom errors, more than they cost in estimation (additional bias/variance). Using this theoretical framework we build a hierarchy search algorithm using greedy additions, we detail its benefit in different data regimes, including abstention in common benchmark datasets where no aggregates provides significant performance improvement.

working_papers.title: Scaling Tabular Foundation Models for Credit Scoring
working_papers.summary: Typical datasets in credit scoring applications can reach several hundred thousands to million rows. In this setting, tabular foundation models have been shown to fall off and not conserve their advantage over simpler ML methods. In order to scale these models to datasets several factors larger than their pretraining, we implement and benchmarks several methods to effectively retrieve local context for each test row or cluster while balancing bias and variance.

working_papers.title: Resolving the Duplicate-Feature Paradox with ReSHAP: A Redundancy-Weighted Generalization of Shapley Attribution
working_papers.authors: Adam Kurpisz, Jens Reil, Lucia T. Gomez, Branka H. Misheva
working_papers.summary:
Shapley-value–based feature attribution methods are widely used to explain machine learning model predictions. However, when features are duplicated or highly correlated, their total attribution can be unfairly inflated, diminishing the attribution assigned to other important features. This paradox arises because traditional Shapley-based methods allocate joint contributions equally across all participating features, regardless of redundancy or informational overlap.

In this work, we propose ReSHAP, a redundancy-aware generalization of Shapley attribution that systematically resolves the attribution consequences of the duplicate-feature paradox. ReSHAP adjusts the allocation of credit within feature coalitions by down-weighting features that contribute redundant information. We begin by proving that no existing attribution method can simultaneously satisfy equal division and redundancy-invariance, even in instances without redundant features. This reveals a fundamental trade-off in designing fair attribution methods. Building on this insight, ReSHAP redefines how Shapley values are computed by redistributing interaction terms across feature subsets using a recursive weighting scheme, using only the standard value function without additional distributional assumptions. We support our theoretical findings with illustrative examples and experiments, highlighting the practical effectiveness of ReSHAP.

working_papers.title: Applications of Interpretable and Explainable Machine Learning in Insurance Pricing
working_papers.authors: Jens Reil, Axel Pison, Marcos R. Machado
working_papers.subjects: Insurance pricing; Non-life; Explainable AI; XAI; SHAP; LIME; Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning
working_papers.summary: This paper examines the application of interpretable and explainable machine learning (ML) to motor-insurance claim frequency and severity modeling, using generalized linear models (GLMs) as actuarial benchmarks. LightGBM, XGBoost, and a multi-layer perceptron are compared with Poisson and Gamma GLMs on data from a Dutch insurer. The study reports predictive-error measures and illustrates model behavior using SHAP and LIME, complemented by semi-structured interviews with five insurance professionals. The observed performance differences are small and depend on the model and metric: the MLP attains a lower mean absolute error than the GLM for both tasks but a slightly higher root mean squared error for claim frequency. The explanation analyses illustrate model-specific feature contributions, while the interviews identify transparency, validation, and governance concerns relevant to practical adoption. The study provides a case-based comparison of actuarial and ML methods and highlights the additional validation required before their operational use in insurance pricing.

working_papers.title: Evaluating Explainable Artificial Intelligence Methods for Financial Time Series Forecasting
working_papers.authors: Jens Reil, Branka H. Misheva, Lucia T. Gomez, Adam Kurpisz, Laura Spierdijk
working_papers.subjects: Forecasting; Explainable AI; XAI; Volatility; Financial market; Stock market; Stylized facts
working_papers.summary: This paper investigates the reliability of existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods in financial time series forecasting, with a particular focus on stock market volatility. Using a controlled experimental framework based on synthetic time series, the study examines how financial characteristics such as volatility clustering, heavy tails, temporal dependence, and structural regime changes affect the accuracy, stability, and faithfulness of explanations generated by commonly used XAI methods, including SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients. By incorporating established volatility forecasting approaches and progressively introducing realistic financial complexities, the study aims to distinguish model predictive performance from explanation quality. The framework is planned to subsequently be extended to real financial data.

working_papers.title: Can Large Language Models Construct Risk-Appropriate and Efficient Portfolios?
working_papers.authors: Jens Reil; Mohamed Faid; Julius Kooistra
working_papers.subjects: Large Language Models; LLM; Stock Market; Investing; Digital Finance
working_papers.summary: This paper investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to construct investment portfolios that align with individual investor risk preferences while maintaining financial efficiency. The study evaluates portfolio recommendations generated by multiple LLMs across different investor risk profiles. The recommended portfolios are assessed against the theoretical efficient frontier derived from Modern Portfolio Theory, examining their risk-return characteristics, diversification, and efficiency. By incorporating quantitative measures of portfolio efficiency, risk alignment, and utility regret, the study aims to distinguish between an LLM's ability to understand investor preferences and its ability to construct financially efficient portfolios. Ultimately, the paper seeks to evaluate the reliability and limitations of LLM-generated investment advice.

working_papers.title: Developing a Scale of Public Explanation Needs for AI-Assisted Financial Applications
working_papers.authors: Patri ia Marcella Evite; Maria Iannario
working_papers.summary: To the best of our knowledge, there is limited psychometric evidence concerning information needs in a questionnaire for eliciting XAI requirements. It consequently remains unclear whether preferences for different categories of explanation content reflect a general explanation-needs construct, several related dimensions, or a profile of distinct information requirements. The present study addresses this gap by developing and psychometrically evaluating a scale of public explanation needs using survey responses from 503 responses with Item Response Theory (IRT).

working_papers.title: Reciprocity Propensity Scores: An ML-based Framework for Non-monetary Economies
working_papers.authors: Patricia Marcella Evite; Doina Bucur; Owen Chaffard; Will Ruddick
working_papers.subjects: blockchain, explainable ai, forecasting, community vouchers
working_papers.summary:
The paper's goal is two-fold. First, we aim to create a baseline reference for so-called perfect balance in reciprocal relationships, where we trace a person's activity from the transactions whether they have both given and received help from another user. In monetary transactions, this can be akin to a loan repayment. Second, based on the first objective's result, we will predict the users who are likely to reciprocate. To get the most accurate results, we will compare the performance of a suite of inherently interpretable and blackbox models. In the case of the latter, an explainable AI (XAI) is added to create an actionable result for the user and our partner NGO Grassroots Economics, accordingly. 

Our contribution is a quantitative complement to evaluation systems for financial credit in humanitarian contexts answering multiple calls for research such as Aiken et al. (2022).
